text: A mint-time verifier: warn when what an author wrote disagrees with what the tool captured

This design proposes that `fact`, `claim` and `prose` compare the text the author just wrote against the evidence the tool already holds, and say so in the tool result when the two disagree. The comparison is a model call, not a string operation, and it happens at the moment of writing rather than in a later grounding round.

The whole proposal stands on one inherited argument. `scope.rs` exists because the project's flagship `Domain ⊆ Extent` check was abandoned as vacuous: with one author supplying both sides, the sides agreed byte-for-byte about four times in five, and independence rather than capture was what moved that number. What rescued the comparison was making one side structural — an extent is captured by `look`/`run`, with deliberately no flag to type one in, while a note is authored. Two different acts, so the comparison cannot be made vacuous by one hand writing both sides. That construction is not specific to locations. A claim's proposition is authored; the output of the facts it cites was captured under the same no-typed-input rule. The independence transfers intact, which is what makes a semantic version of the same comparison worth building at all.

It is also aimed at a gap the existing check names for itself. `scope.rs` reports that of the two overreaching facts in the memo that motivated it, it catches one — the one that named a file and line range it never opened. The other asserted that a client "mirrors the server's" walk while its extent covered only the client, and is missed because it names no location at all: invisible, in the module's own words, to any check of that shape. The one refinement tried and rejected failed for the same reason recorded in the same place — naming a symbol the code you read calls is normal, concluding about what that symbol does is the failure, and those two are not distinguishable by string matching. A check that compares meaning is the check that residual describes. This design is `scope.rs` for meaning rather than for location, and it inherits `scope.rs`'s posture along with its argument: human-owed, never a refusal.
## The surface

The mint results already carry two findings of this family, and they set the register. `fact` returns `attention`, a top-level array whose entries say a note names a location the extent does not cover; `claim` returns `overlap`, the ids and shared extent keys of facts the author looked at and did not cite. Both are shaped as fields rather than sentences on the stated ground that the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice. The verifier's finding belongs in the same place for the same reason — and, following the same doc comment, for the reason that only the author, at the moment of writing, can still cheaply tell context from conclusion.

It should not, however, be a third array. `attention` and `overlap` are computed per call out of workspace state that is already on disk, so for them an empty array and an absent one carry the same information: nothing was found. A model call can fail, be switched off, time out, or be refused for want of a key, and in every one of those states "found nothing" is a different fact from "did not look". So `verify` is an object with a mandatory `status` — one of `ok`, `off`, `unavailable`, `timeout`, `unauthorized` — and a `findings` array that is only meaningful under `ok`. A caller that branches on `verify.status` cannot mistake a silent outage for a clean bill.

One field in that object is not optional and has no counterpart in the precedent. `attention` and `overlap` recompute to the same answer every time, because their inputs are files on disk. This check does not: the eval measured, on identical input at temperature 0, reasoning length swinging between 516 and 2000 tokens, with the draws that reach the token ceiling returning an empty response body. Two identical mints can therefore warn differently, or warn once and stay silent the next time. A reader who sees a third finding sitting beside two deterministic ones will assume parity unless told otherwise, so the object names the model that produced it and carries `deterministic: false` in every response, including the silent ones.
## What the eval settled, and what it did not

The measurement in `scripts/verifier-eval/` decides the shape of the check and deliberately decides nothing about its worth. On fifteen cases run three times, the one-call direct comparison caught thirty-two of thirty-three planted defects and left all twelve sound claims alone for six tenths of a cent; the three-call extract-then-judge pipeline managed twenty-eight of thirty-two and seven of twelve for nearly nine times the money. Better on both axes at a ninth of the cost is not a close call, and the hypothesis that extracting first and comparing second would beat a single call did not survive contact with the numbers. The direct comparison is therefore the default.

What the same README says about itself is the more important half. The cases are synthetic, none taken from a real memo; the set is small and was written by the same process that then measured against it; one case was discovered to be mislabeled only because the model disagreed with it, which is a warning about the remaining fourteen as much as a reassurance about the model. And the section closes by naming the thing it does not measure at all — whether warning an author earlier removes a grounding round, which is the entire cost argument for the feature. That sentence is the reason this document ends in a gate rather than a build order.

The pipeline it beat is nevertheless kept as a selectable mode, and the reason has nothing to do with its score. Its accuracy was measured on an earlier fourteen-case set and cannot be laid beside the fifteen-case columns at all. What it has is a property the winner cannot acquire: its findings are re-derivable by anyone holding the two extracted records, with no model in the loop, while the direct comparison's are re-derivable only by asking a model again. For an author who needs a finding to survive being handed to someone without an API key, that is worth three calls and nine times the money — but it is a deliberate selection, never the default.
## Configuration, and the key that never lands in it

`config.rs` sets an admission test before it offers a registry: every setting in that file must be visible in the output it affects, and a setting that cannot be shown that way should not be added. The grounding floor passes because it is printed beside the owed list it produced. The verifier's settings pass for the same reason and by the same mechanism — the `verify` object names its status, its model and its non-determinism in every response it returns, so the result carries its own configuration on the page. Five keys follow: `verify.enabled`, `verify.model`, `verify.approach`, `verify.timeout_ms` and `verify.verbs`, each one entry in the existing static registry with its own `accepts` rule. They need neither a new scope nor a new file. The absent project scope stays absent for the reason the module already gives: such a file would have to be written inside the repository under design, where the workspace module refuses to write at all.

The API key is not among them and must come from the environment, because config files are shared, committed and pasted into issues. Most of that rule is already enforced without new code: there is no `verify.api_key` entry, `set` resolves every key through the registry and refuses what it does not find, and the refusal lists the known keys so an author who tried is told what they could have written instead. One gap remains, and it is at the value level rather than the key level — `verify.model` is a string key and would cheerfully accept a credential pasted into it. The strict-when-set half of the module's asymmetry is exactly the right hook: a new `accepts` rule that refuses a credential-shaped value at write time. This does not breach the rule that refusals are format-level, since `set` already refuses on value shape by construction, and a refusal at `config set` can never suppress a mint.
## The crate property this breaks

`lib.rs` pins two properties across the whole crate, and this feature makes one of them false the day it lands: there are no network calls anywhere, which the dependency set enforces rather than the prose. The parenthesis is the part that matters. Once an HTTP client is linked the dependency set enforces nothing, and a softened version of the same sentence would be prose impersonating an invariant. The module has already been through this once and says so in its preamble — a single sentence about the whole crate was wrong for months, which is why the write list is stated per command — so the replacement takes the form the file already prefers. `fact`, `claim` and `prose` may make one outbound call to the configured provider, and only when the feature is enabled with a key present in the environment; `check`, `brief`, `query`, `review`, `workspaces`, `render`, `record` and `config` make none. The second pinned property, that nothing here ever executes a command named by a document, survives intact, and it is the reason `check` appears on the second list rather than the first.
## Which partition it belongs to

Neither. `report.rs` holds two arrays of canonical category names, one per partition, and they exist as a single enumerated source because three hand-maintained copies of the same lists had already drifted apart — the module's scope strings and the `check` tool description are both generated from them. So the arrays are not a taxonomy of findings in general; they are a statement of what `check` covers. This check does not run inside `check`, does not enter the record, the memo, the snapshot or the evidence ledger, and cannot be recomputed by a reader holding the document. Adding it to either array would make a scope string promise coverage `check` does not have, which is the exact failure the arrays were introduced to end. The warning lives in the mint result and nowhere else.
## Where findings persist

A workspace already keeps a log of things that happened but are not records — `refusals.log` — and a sibling `verify.log` is the natural home for findings an author scrolled past, particularly since the gate below needs a corpus to measure against. But `refusals.log` is exactly the wrong sibling to copy in one respect: it is an entry in `SNAPSHOT_FILES`, so it is shipped into `<memo>.tetel/` on every render. A log of model output shipped that way would put non-reproducible text inside the snapshot, which is the one place this design has promised never to reach. What rescues the idea is that the shipping list is an allowlist and not a denylist, each entry carrying a comment arguing for its own inclusion. A new workspace file is therefore withheld by default and can only start shipping when someone writes that argument for it. `verify.log` stays out of the snapshot by construction rather than by intention, and needs no mechanism to keep it there.
## What is compared, and what it costs

Mints are instant today, and the eval's calls were not. The cost is easy to underestimate because the unit paying it is the tool call rather than the record: in the largest memo on disk, the append-only logs hold two hundred and seventy-seven lines across facts, claims and prose, of which a hundred and fourteen claim lines resolve to thirty-nine distinct claims. Two thirds of claim traffic is revision. Verifying every line of a run like that is tens of minutes of added wall-clock, against a few cents of spend — so the design is shaped by the clock and not by the bill. Three consequences follow. The mint commits before the verifier runs, so a slow provider delays the reply and never the record. The wait is bounded by `verify.timeout_ms` and reports `status: timeout` when it expires. And a revision that does not change the text being compared makes no call at all, which is where most of the volume lives.

The same budget decides which of the three verbs is checked. `claim` is on by default and the other two are selectable and off. That is not a hedge: `claim` is the only verb whose accuracy has been measured, since the eval's cases were written to imitate the shape of a tetel claim beside its captured evidence. `fact` already has the cheap half of its check for free and deterministically — `scope` compares the locations a note names against the extent, and the semantic residue is the smaller of the two halves that module describes. `prose` is the awkward one. It is the highest-volume verb of the three in the memo measured, at a hundred and thirty log lines, and prose-against-propositions is a different comparison from the one the eval ran, with no numbers behind it whatsoever. Turning it on by default would spend the largest share of the latency budget on the least-evidenced comparison. It stays available, because the worst defect this project has recorded entered through prose, and it stays off until something measures it.

text: ## The modification surface

Three symbols are declared as modification targets and each was censused across the whole worktree before being named here. `fact_result` is defined once and called twice in production, from the minted and the revised arms of the `fact` tool, so one `verify` key added to that builder reaches both outcomes and no other caller; its only other appearances in the tree are a same-named local variable inside a test. `known_keys` occurs twice in the entire worktree, both inside the config module, and `Accepts` six times, likewise all inside it, with exactly one variant in use today. The config work is therefore self-contained: new registry entries, new `Accepts` variants, and matching arms in the validator and in the message that tells an author what they could have written instead. Nothing outside that module reads either symbol.
## The degradation contract

Every terminal state of the provider call maps to exactly one `status`, and the mapping is total. Disabled by configuration is `off`. No key in the environment is `unauthorized`. A transport failure or a non-2xx reply is `unavailable`. Expiry of the configured budget is `timeout`. Only a well-formed answer that genuinely contains no finding is `ok` with an empty `findings` array. The awkward case is the truncated one, and it is the case the eval already met: a draw that reaches the token ceiling comes back with a body of length zero, which is trivially easy to treat as a clean result. It is `unavailable`. The eval's own harness made precisely this mistake in its first form — an errored row recorded as an unflagged one, which reads as a miss on a defective case and as a correct silence on a sound one, wrong in both directions at once — and the fix there was to give errors their own column entering no denominator. The same discipline is what `status` is for here. In all of these states the mint has already committed, so nothing in this contract can fail a mint or move an exit code.

A finding's contents matter more than its container, because the author receiving it is usually an agent and an agent acts on warnings. A false positive that arrives as a verdict gets a correct claim "fixed". The eval has a measured instance of exactly this: the pipeline's false positives were all one failure mode, and the recorded one reported that the evidence contained no pin name or binding against evidence whose lines 425-436 are the pin computation. Stated as a verdict, that can only be accepted or ignored. Stated as a quotation — this clause, judged against these captured lines — its wrongness is visible in a single step to anyone holding the memo. So an entry names the clause it is judging, the fact id, and the span of captured output it was compared against, all quoted, and carries no confidence score. A number invites deference; a quotation invites checking, and checking is the only response that is safe when the check is wrong.
## The gate

Nothing described above should be built before the retrodiction test, and the corpus for it is already on disk. Seven memos each carry an evidence log beside a snapshot. The claim logs record every Create and Revise with a timestamp and the wording carried at that moment, so each claim's text as it stood at first render can be reconstructed exactly; the evidence logs are in-toto statements whose subject is a claim id and whose predicate carries a verdict. Across all seven there are 786 rows: 578 supports, 185 qualifies, 23 refutes. The test is therefore fully specified before it is written — for each of the 208 non-supporting verdicts, take the claim's first-render wording, run the verifier over it against the facts it cited then, and ask two questions: did it flag, and did the flag name the same defect the grounder named. Both denominators are known in advance, which is what lets the threshold be fixed now instead of argued about once the numbers are in.

Two outcomes kill the feature, and both are declared here rather than after the run. If fewer than a quarter of the 23 refutes are surfaced on their first-render wording, the verifier does not catch the findings that actually force a revision round, and the cost argument for the whole thing collapses on the only corpus capable of testing it. If more than one in ten of the 578 supporting claims is flagged at its first-render wording, it is a steering hazard: each of those flags is an invitation to an agent to damage a claim that was already sound, and there are enough of them to outweigh anything gained elsewhere. Either result kills it on its own. A disappointing showing on the 185 qualifies does not, because a qualification is frequently a legitimate narrowing of scope rather than a defect the author should have avoided, and treating that bucket as the target would reward a verifier that flags everything.

The register travels with the finding rather than only in the tool description. The precedent does both — each `attention` entry carries its own `guidance` string, while the descriptions around it set the tone in the words "It is not an error — read it and decide" — and the reason to prefer the payload is that a caller may never re-read a description it loaded once. Putting the sentence in the entry also keeps it inside the single builder this design already modifies, instead of in a second place that can drift from it. `attention` goes further and shares its advice text verbatim with the CLI so the two surfaces cannot disagree about the same finding; `verify` should be produced the same way.

A workspace already keeps a log of things that happened but are not records — `refusals.log` — and a sibling `verify.log` is the natural home for findings an author scrolled past. But `refusals.log` is exactly the wrong sibling to copy in one respect: it is an entry in `SNAPSHOT_FILES`, so it is shipped into `<memo>.tetel/` on every render. A log of model output shipped that way would put non-reproducible text inside the snapshot, which is the one place this design has promised never to reach. What rescues the idea is that the shipping list is an allowlist and not a denylist, each entry carrying a comment arguing for its own inclusion. A new workspace file is therefore withheld by default and can only start shipping when someone writes that argument for it. `verify.log` stays out of the snapshot by construction rather than by intention, and needs no mechanism to keep it there.

text:
This design proposes that `fact`, `claim` and `prose` compare the text the author just wrote against the evidence the tool already holds, and say so in the tool result when the two disagree. The comparison is a model call, not a string operation, and it is triggered at the moment of writing rather than in a later grounding round.

The whole proposal stands on one inherited argument, and on getting the inheritance right. `scope.rs` exists because the project's flagship `Domain ⊆ Extent` check was abandoned as vacuous: with one author supplying both sides, the sides agreed byte-for-byte about four times in five, and independence rather than capture was what moved that number. What rescued the comparison was making one side structural — an extent is captured by `look`/`run`, with deliberately no flag to type one in, while a note is authored. That construction has two halves, and only the first is free here. The captured side cannot be typed: an author can no more type a cited fact's captured output than they can type an extent. But the captured side is also complete — `look` and `run` record what was actually opened — and for a claim the captured side would be whatever the author chose to cite. An overreaching proposition could then be made to agree with its evidence by citing only the facts that agree with it, and the verifier would see no disagreement because the disagreeing evidence never entered the comparison. That is the author's diligence doing the work again, which is the failure the whole construction exists to avoid.

tetel already knows this choice is unreliable, which is why creating a claim hands back an overlap report: every fact touching the same files that the author did not cite. So the comparison is defined over the cited facts together with that overlap set. Both are on disk at claim time and neither costs a new mechanism — the overlap report is computed inside `create`, one line before the claim event is appended, from a load of every fact in the workspace. With that union as the captured side, neither half can be typed and neither can be narrowed by selection, and the independence transfers intact. That is what makes a semantic version of the comparison worth building at all.
why: C1 was qualified and then strengthened: the keystone paragraph asserted a clean transfer of the independence construction, but only one of its two properties survives for a claim unless the comparison runs against the cited facts plus the overlap set. The paragraph now carries the property that does not transfer for free, and the design decision that restores it.

text: `lib.rs` pins two properties across the whole crate, and this feature makes one of them false the day it lands: there are no network calls anywhere, which the dependency set enforces rather than the prose. The parenthesis is the part that matters. Once an HTTP client is linked the dependency set enforces nothing, and a softened version of the same sentence would be prose impersonating an invariant. The module has already been through this once and says so in its preamble — a single sentence about the whole crate was wrong for months, which is why the write list is stated per command — so the replacement takes the form the file already prefers, and it has to cover all fifteen commands the file lists or it reintroduces the same defect through the enumeration instead of the generalisation. Three reach: `fact`, `claim` and `prose` may make one outbound call to the configured provider, and only when the feature is enabled with a key present in the environment. Eleven make none: `check`, `brief`, `query`, `review`, `workspaces`, `look`, `target`, `transplant`, `render`, `record` and `config`. `run` gets its own line, because neither list is true of it. The crate makes no call of its own for `run`; `run` spawns the command the author typed, in the author's own session, and that process can reach the network exactly as anything else the author runs in a terminal can. The categorical sentence never had to say this, being about the crate's own calls; a per-command row does. The second pinned property, that nothing here ever executes a command named by a document, survives intact — `run` executes what the author types, never what a memo contains — and it is the reason `check` is on the eleven and not the three.
why: C9's replacement row was short by four commands; the paragraph carried the same eleven-command list, leaving `look`, `run`, `target` and `transplant` unmentioned, and `run` needs a line of its own because it spawns an author-typed process.

text:
Mints are instant today, and the eval's calls were not. The cost is easy to underestimate because the unit paying it is the tool call rather than the record: in the largest memo on disk, the append-only logs hold two hundred and seventy-seven lines across facts, claims and prose, of which a hundred and fourteen claim lines resolve to thirty-nine distinct claims. Two thirds of claim traffic is revision. Verifying every line of a run like that is tens of minutes of added wall-clock against a few cents of spend, so the design is shaped by the clock and not by the bill.

Committing the mint before the call is necessary and not sufficient, because a mint result is one object. `fact_result` carries `attention`, `folded` and `refused_since_previous_fact` in the same payload the verifier would join; the claim result carries `overlap`. All of those are deterministic findings that arrive with certainty today only because a mint is instant, and putting a provider call in front of the reply makes every one of them contingent on the provider: a client whose own request timeout is shorter than `verify.timeout_ms`, or an author who interrupts, gets the record committed and a note-outside-extent warning thrown away that no model was ever involved in producing.

So nothing in the reply path waits. The mint result returns immediately, carrying only what can be decided without a call. The comparison runs after the reply, and its finding is delivered on the author's next authoring call in that workspace, and appended to `verify.log`. This is not a new idea in this codebase: a mint already reports the refusals recorded in the window before it, through one helper shared by the CLI and the MCP surface so the two cannot drift on which refusals a mint reports. The remaining rules follow. `verify.timeout_ms` bounds a mint's verification end to end rather than a single HTTP attempt, and since it no longer sits in front of a reply it can be generous. A revision that does not change the text being compared makes no call at all, which is where most of the volume lives. The price is that a warning lands one tool call after the writing it concerns; what is bought is the removal of the entire latency budget from the author's critical path, and one tool call later is still many rounds earlier than a grounding pass.
why: C12 was qualified: committing the mint first protects the record but leaves the deterministic payload — attention, folded, refused_since_previous_fact, overlap — riding in the same single result as the model call. The paragraph now carries the stronger shape: nothing in the reply path waits, and the finding is delivered on the next authoring call, the way refusals from the previous window already are.

text: Every terminal state of the provider call maps to exactly one `status`, and the mapping has to be total or it reproduces the defect it exists to prevent. Disabled by configuration is `off`. No key in the environment is `unauthorized`. A transport failure or a non-2xx reply is `unavailable`. Expiry of the budget is `timeout`. A truncated draw is the case the eval already met — reaching the token ceiling comes back with a body of length zero, which is trivially easy to treat as a clean result — and it is `unavailable`, never `ok`. The state an earlier drafting of this contract missed is the one that is hardest to see: a perfectly good 2xx reply, non-empty and non-truncated, whose content is not a usable answer. The harness this design borrows its contract from meets that state in three distinct shapes — no brace-delimited substring in the body at all, a substring that fails `json.loads`, and a decoded object whose verdict is outside the three permitted values — and none of them is a transport failure, a non-2xx, an empty body or a truncation. All three are `unparsable`. `ok` is reachable only from a decoded verdict in the fixed vocabulary, which is what keeps an unreadable answer from arriving as a clean bill with an empty `findings` array. That is precisely the mistake the eval's own harness made in its first form — an errored row recorded as an unflagged one, which reads as a miss on a defective case and a correct silence on a sound one, wrong in both directions at once — and the fix there was to give errors their own column entering no denominator. `status` is the same discipline. The budget's unit is stated with it: `verify.timeout_ms` bounds one mint's verification end to end, across every retry, because the harness's own call retries up to three times with a tripled cap, and a per-attempt bound would quietly license three times the declared spend. And since the call runs after the mint result has already gone back, every state here is reported on a later call and none of them can fail a mint, delay a reply or move an exit code.
why: C15 was refuted: a 2xx, non-empty, non-truncated body carrying no usable verdict mapped to none of the six states and fell through to `ok` with empty findings — the very defect the paragraph cites as its justification. The paragraph now carries the `unparsable` state, its three measured shapes, and the timeout budget's unit.

text: The mint results already carry two findings of this family, and they set the register. `fact` returns `attention`, a top-level array whose entries say a note names a location the extent does not cover; `claim` returns `overlap`, the ids and shared extent keys of facts the author looked at and did not cite. Both are shaped as fields rather than sentences on the stated ground that the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice. The verifier's finding belongs in the same place for the same reason — and, following the same doc comment, for the reason that only the author, near the moment of writing, can still cheaply tell context from conclusion.
why: C3 now carries a two-part status vocabulary, because the reply that triggers a verification cannot report its outcome. The paragraph pair describing the surface has to say which reply carries what.

text:
The mint results already carry two findings of this family, and they set the register. `fact` returns `attention`, a top-level array whose entries say a note names a location the extent does not cover; `claim` returns `overlap`, the ids and shared extent keys of facts the author looked at and did not cite. Both are shaped as fields rather than sentences on the stated ground that the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice. The verifier's finding belongs in the same place for the same reason — and, following the same doc comment, for the reason that only the author, near the moment of writing, can still cheaply tell context from conclusion.

It should not, however, be a third array. `attention` and `overlap` are computed per call out of workspace state that is already on disk, so for them an empty array and an absent one carry the same information: nothing was found. A model call can be switched off, be refused for want of a key, fail in transport, time out, or come back unreadable, and in every one of those states "found nothing" is a different fact from "did not look". A verification also outlives the reply that triggered it, so the result carrying the mint cannot report the verification's outcome at all. Only an object holds both halves. `verify` therefore has a mandatory `status`: the reply that triggers a verification says `off`, `unauthorized` or `queued`, each decidable without a call, and the reply that delivers one says `ok`, `unavailable`, `timeout` or `unparsable`, naming the mint its findings concern, since that is no longer the id sitting beside them. `findings` is meaningful only under `ok`. A caller that branches on `verify.status` cannot mistake a silent outage, a disabled feature or a call still in flight for a clean bill.
why: My previous revision of this block silently dropped its second paragraph, the one arguing `verify` must be an object rather than a third array. Restoring it, and updating it for C3's two-part status vocabulary: the reply that triggers a verification reports only what can be decided without a call, and the reply that delivers one names the mint its findings concern.

text: Which raises the question the previous paragraph does not answer: nothing so far makes the quotation true. A quoted span in a finding is a string a model produced, recovered from free text by a regular expression and a JSON parse, and a fabricated quotation is strictly worse than a bare verdict — it sends a recipient to check against text that does not exist, so the one response that is safe when the check is wrong is the response it defeats. This repository already owns the fix and applies it to exactly this kind of authored claim about captured evidence. `Fact::quotes` decides whether a string is a verbatim substring of a single observation's captured output: byte for byte, with nothing normalised, and single rather than joined so that a span straddling two observations cannot be assembled out of text that was never contiguous in anything anyone looked at. It is what makes `transplant` refuse a premise that is not the donor's own words, and it is a plain substring search — no model, no network, no knowledge of the language it is reading. So `verify_block` puts every finding's quoted span through it before that finding enters the payload. A span it accepts ships as a quotation. A span it rejects is dropped, and its finding is downgraded to one that carries no evidence quotation and says so. Nothing is refused and no mint is affected; the check runs on the model's output rather than the author's, and all it withholds is the authority a quotation carries from text that did not come from the captured record.

Volume decides which of the three verbs is checked, and evidence decides it twice over. `claim` is on by default and the other two are selectable and off. That is not a hedge: `claim` is the only verb whose accuracy has been measured, since the eval's cases were written to imitate the shape of a tetel claim beside its captured evidence. `fact` already has the cheap half of its check for free and deterministically — `scope` compares the locations a note names against the extent, and the semantic residue is the smaller of the two halves that module describes. `prose` is the awkward one. It is the highest-volume verb of the three in the memo measured, at a hundred and thirty log lines against a hundred and fourteen for claims and thirty-three for facts, and prose-against-propositions is a different comparison from the one the eval ran, with no numbers behind it whatsoever. Defaulting it on would spend the largest share of the budget on the least-evidenced comparison, so it stays available and stays off until something measures it.
why: The preceding paragraph now takes latency off the author's critical path, so "the same budget" read as a reference to something the design had just removed. The verb selection rests on volume and on which comparison has been measured, which is what C13 says.

text:
This design proposes that `fact`, `claim` and `prose` compare the text the author just wrote against the evidence the tool already holds, and say so in the tool result when the two disagree. The comparison is a model call, not a string operation, and it is triggered at the moment of writing rather than in a later grounding round.

The whole proposal stands on one inherited argument, and on getting the inheritance right. `scope.rs` exists because the project's flagship `Domain ⊆ Extent` check was abandoned as vacuous: with one author supplying both sides, the sides agreed byte-for-byte about four times in five, and independence rather than capture was what moved that number. What rescued the comparison was making one side structural — an extent is captured by `look`/`run`, and there is deliberately no flag to type one in, while a note is authored. That construction has two halves, and only the first is free here. The captured side cannot be typed: an author can no more type a cited fact's captured output than they can type an extent. But the captured side is also complete — `look` and `run` record what was actually opened — and for a claim the captured side would be whatever the author chose to cite. An overreaching proposition could then be made to agree with its evidence by citing only the facts that agree with it, and the verifier would see no disagreement because the disagreeing evidence never entered the comparison. That is the author's diligence doing the work again, which is the failure the whole construction exists to avoid.

tetel already knows this choice is unreliable, which is why creating a claim hands back an overlap report: every fact touching the same files that the author did not cite. So the comparison is defined over the cited facts together with that overlap set. Both are on disk at claim time and neither costs a new mechanism — inside `create`, the overlap report is computed at `src/claims.rs:136` and the claim event is appended at `:140`, four lines and two statements later, from a load of every fact in the workspace, and the set is handed back in the same outcome. With that union as the captured side, neither half can be typed and neither can be narrowed by selection, and the independence transfers intact. That is what makes a semantic version of the comparison worth building at all.
why: Behind the C1 revision: the quoted phrase is scope.rs's "and there is deliberately no flag to type one in", and overlap_report runs four lines and two statements before the append, not one line before it.

text: The register travels with the finding rather than only in the tool description. The precedent carries it in both places, but not in the same words, and the split is the argument rather than an embarrassment to it. In the payload, each `attention` entry carries its own `guidance` string, built beside the finding by `scope::advice` and hedged in that function's own terms — "Fine if that's context. If it's a conclusion about {}, you have not read it here". The crisper sentence, "It is not an error — read it and decide", is not `attention`'s at all: it belongs to the `claim` tool's description and is about the overlap report. So the sharpest statement of the register sits on the surface a caller loads once and may never read again, while the finding that needs it arrives alone — which is the reason to put a register string in the finding. What the argument cannot lean on is a claim that the guidance rides along inside one builder for free. It does not: `fact_result` builds the two `fact` results, while `claim` and `prose` results are assembled by inline literals at their own sites, and the default-on verb is one of the two `fact_result` never touches. The drift this raises is real and has to be answered directly, so `verify` is added at each of the three sites and the guidance text, the status vocabulary and the non-determinism marker are all produced by the shared `verify_block` helper rather than restated per verb. That is the discipline `scope::advice` already enforces for `attention`, one definition reaching both the MCP payload at `src/mcp.rs:185` and the CLI at `src/main.rs:650` and `:657`, so two surfaces cannot disagree about one finding.
why: Behind the C19 revision: "It is not an error — read it and decide" is the `claim` tool description's sentence about the overlap report, not `attention`'s and not `scope::advice`'s. The corrected attribution strengthens the paragraph's own argument rather than weakening it.

text: `config.rs` sets an admission test before it offers a registry: every setting in that file must be visible in the output it affects, and a setting that cannot be shown that way should not be added. The grounding floor passes because it is printed beside the owed list it produced. Five keys are wanted here — `verify.enabled`, `verify.model`, `verify.approach`, `verify.timeout_ms` and `verify.verbs` — and it is worth being exact about which of them an echo of status, model and non-determinism would actually cover. `verify.enabled` shows up as a status of `off` and `verify.model` by name; `verify.timeout_ms` would surface only in the one state that trips it, `verify.verbs` only by inference from an absence, and `verify.approach` — the choice between two materially different mechanisms — nowhere at all, so a reader could not tell which of them produced the finding in front of them. Under the rule as the module states it, that is a disqualification and not a rough edge. The answer is to widen the echo rather than to keep a key in defiance of the sentence quoted to justify it: `verify_block` writes the effective value of all five into every `verify` object it builds — status, model, approach, timeout and the verb list — beside `deterministic: false`, including on the calls where the setting made nothing happen. Each key is then one entry in the existing static registry with its own `accepts` rule, and each is on the page of every response it affects. They need neither a new scope nor a new file. The absent project scope stays absent for the reason the module already gives: such a file would have to be written inside the repository under design, where the workspace module refuses to write at all.
why: Behind the C8 revision: an echo of status, model and the determinism marker leaves `verify.approach` invisible in the output it affects, which is the disqualification config.rs's own rule pronounces. The echo is widened to all five effective values rather than a key kept in defiance of the quoted rule.

text: A workspace already keeps a log of things that happened but are not records — `refusals.log` — and a sibling `verify.log` is the natural home for findings an author scrolled past. But `refusals.log` is exactly the wrong sibling to copy in one respect: it is an entry in `SNAPSHOT_FILES`, so it is shipped into `<memo>.tetel/` on every render. A log of model output shipped that way would put non-reproducible text inside the snapshot, which is the one place this design has promised never to reach. What rescues the idea is the shape of the list rather than the manners around it: `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an enumeration of ten names, and `write` walks exactly that array and copies exactly those names, so a workspace file whose name is not in it cannot be copied at all. The array says as much about itself — enumerated rather than copied wholesale, so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold rather than an accident of `cp -r`. It would be wrong to lean on the entries' comments for this: only four of the ten carry one, and of the six that do not, only `pending.json` is argued for in the array's doc comment. The comment is a courtesy; the enumeration is the mechanism. So `verify.log` stays out of the snapshot by construction, needs no mechanism to keep it there, and shipping it later would take a deliberate line in that array.
why: Behind the C11 revision: only four of the ten SNAPSHOT_FILES entries carry a justifying comment, so the commenting convention the paragraph relied on is not the file's practice. What enforces the withholding is the enumeration plus `write` copying only names drawn from it.

text: Which of the three verbs is checked by default is the one place this design has to correct the eval's own headline before it can use it. It is tempting to say `claim` is on because `claim` is the verb that was measured. That is false. The fifteen-case set is two files: twelve in-scope cases from `cases.py`, and three from `extra_cases.py`, which opens by saying its cases are aimed at the note-versus-extent check specifically — the `fact` comparison — and every harness builds its run as the in-scope cases plus those three. Two of each run's eleven defective cases and one of its four sound ones are therefore `fact` cases, and the thirty-two of thirty-three and twelve of twelve are sums over both verbs with no per-verb column anywhere in the output. So `fact` has numbers, `claim`'s cannot be separated from them, and the honest reading is that the eval licenses no per-verb accuracy statement at all — a reason for more caution about those columns, not for preferring one verb over another. The default set is decided on coverage and volume instead. `claim` is the comparison nothing in the crate performs today: `attention` reads a note against its own extent, and `overlap` is deliberately ids and shared extent keys rather than notes, so no existing check reads a proposition against the content of the evidence cited for it. `fact` is the one verb already half covered, deterministically and for free, by `scope` — and this design declines to say how large the remaining semantic residue is, because nothing measures it: `scope.rs` reports catching one of the two overreaches that motivated it, which is parity rather than a smaller half, and `extra_cases.py` describes the deterministic check as catching a note that names an unopened file only when that file's name happens not to appear anywhere in the extent string. `fact` stays off because half its work is already done and the rest is unsized, and it is the first verb to turn on when someone sizes it. `prose` stays off for a plainer reason: it is the highest-volume verb of the three in the memo measured, at a hundred and thirty log lines against a hundred and fourteen for claims and thirty-three for facts, and prose-against-propositions is a comparison neither case file contains. Defaulting it on would spend the largest share of the budget on the least-evidenced comparison.
why: Behind the C13 revision: the eval did measure `fact` — three of its fifteen cases are note-versus-extent cases mixed into the same headline — so the "only measured verb" argument is gone and the default set is re-argued from existing coverage and volume. The unsupported "smaller of the two halves" comparison is replaced by what scope.rs and extra_cases.py actually say.

text: Two outcomes kill the feature, and both are declared here rather than after the run. If 7 or more of the 62 claims that carry supports and nothing else are flagged at their first-render wording, it is a steering hazard: each of those flags is an invitation to an agent to damage a claim that was already sound. If 2 or fewer of the 9 refuted claims that have a first-render wording are surfaced with a finding naming the defect a later pass named, the verifier does not catch what forces a revision round, and the cost argument collapses on the only corpus capable of testing it. Both are counts of claims over counts of claims, which an earlier drafting of this gate was not, and the difference is not cosmetic: taken against the 578 supports rows, flagging every sound claim in the corpus scores 10.7 per cent against a ten per cent line, and an eighty-one per cent false-positive rate — fifty flags — passes at 8.7 per cent. Nor is that an artefact of which row count is used: over the 510 supports rows that belong to claims with a first-render wording the same two numerators give 12.2 and 9.8 per cent, and the eighty-one per cent rate still passes. A gate that cannot fail is worse than no gate. The recall side deserves less confidence than the false-positive side, because nine is a small denominator and a single claim moves it eleven points: clearing that line is the absence of a reason to stop, not a reason to build. A disappointing showing on the 60 claims carrying a qualifies is not a kill either, because a qualification is frequently a legitimate narrowing of scope rather than a defect the author should have avoided, and treating that bucket as the target would reward a verifier that flags everything.
why: Behind the C18 revision: 12.1% and 9.9% are 62 and 50 over 510, not over the 578 the sentence names. Over 578 the figures are 10.7% and 8.7%, which still make the point.

text: ## What the gate returned

The test ran over all 125 claims, three draws each, in the configuration six harness iterations settled on: assertions classified before they are checked, the whole claim held in view while each assertion is checked, and the captured side taken as the cited facts together with the overlap set. It returned a split verdict, not a pass. The steering-hazard line passes and passes clearly — four of the sixty-two claims a later pass only ever supported were flagged, against a line drawn at seven. The recall line fires. Nine claims in the corpus were refuted by a later pass and had a first-render wording to feed the verifier; three of those were flagged, and two of the three carried a finding naming the defect the refutation named. Two is the kill. The third flag is worth its own sentence, because it is the kind of thing a bare count hides: on tet61's C15 the verifier found a real arithmetic error in a census — thirty-two occurrences where the claim said thirty-one — while both of that claim's refutations were about a modification surface that was incomplete. A correct finding about the wrong defect counts on the flag column and not on the naming one, which is the strict reading and the one the gate declared. `gate_result.py --show-refuted` prints all nine claims with their refutation notes and the verifier's findings beside them, because "named the same defect" is a reading rather than a measurement, and a design that declares its kill conditions in advance owes the reader the means to disagree with how one was scored.

The feature is nevertheless built, and the honest way to say why is to name what the fired line tested rather than to argue with the number. It tested whether the verifier catches what forces a revision round, because that is the whole of the cost argument: warn the author at the mint and one grounding pass need not happen. Two of nine does not support that, and no reading of the corpus rescues it — so the cost argument is withdrawn from this design rather than defended, and nothing downstream may lean on it. What the same run also measured is a different proposition, one the gate never made a condition: of the 125 claims, 23 were flagged, and 19 of those were claims a later pass did not simply support. Four flags in the whole corpus land on a claim that was already sound. A finding that is right five times in six, costs about a hundredth of a cent, arrives where the fix is one re-look rather than one revision round, blocks nothing and can be ignored without consequence does not need to remove a pass to be worth its price. That is the ground the feature is built on, and it is a weaker ground than the one this document opened with. Both the fired line and this replacement stay in the record, because a kill condition that fires and is then overridden is worth less than one never declared unless what overrode it is stated as plainly as the line itself.

One population is left unresolved, and it is the largest of the three. Sixty claims in the corpus carry at least one qualifies, and eighteen of them were flagged. The gate declined in advance to make that bucket a kill condition, on the ground that a qualification is frequently a legitimate narrowing of scope rather than a defect the author should have avoided — and that decision, made before the run, is what now leaves eighteen flags with no verdict attached. They cannot be scored against this corpus in either direction: the ground truth that would separate a finding a grader would have welcomed at the mint from noise an agent would have acted on is exactly what a qualifies verdict does not record. No re-run changes that, because the missing thing is not a measurement but a distinction the source data never drew. The measurement that settles it is prospective — the verifier's flags recorded beside the graders' verdicts on memos written after it ships — which makes instrumenting the feature from its first day part of building it rather than a later refinement, and makes the eighteen a reason to keep the default verb set small until the numbers come in.

The measurement in `scripts/verifier-eval/` decides the shape of the check and deliberately decides nothing about its worth. On fifteen cases run three times, the one-call direct comparison caught thirty-two of thirty-three planted defects and left all twelve sound claims alone for six tenths of a cent; the three-call extract-then-judge pipeline managed twenty-eight of thirty-two and seven of twelve for nearly nine times the money. Better on both axes at a ninth of the cost is not a close call, and the hypothesis that extracting first and comparing second would beat a single call did not survive contact with the numbers. The direct comparison is therefore the default.

What the same README says about itself is the more important half. The cases are synthetic, none taken from a real memo; the set is small and was written by the same process that then measured against it; one case was discovered to be mislabeled only because the model disagreed with it, which is a warning about the remaining fourteen as much as a reassurance about the model. And the section closes by naming the thing it does not measure at all — whether warning an author earlier removes a grounding round, which is the entire cost argument for the feature. That sentence is the reason nothing here was built before a retrodiction test on real memos, and the last section of this document records what that test returned: the cost argument named in this paragraph is the one thing it did not survive.
